item.title: Mukta bodha intro
item.description: Śāmbhava The family of traditions variously labelled Śāmbhava, Ṣaḍanvayaśāmbhava, Śāmbhavī vidyā, and forth, are perhaps the least well understood of the living tantric lineages that claim a textual foundation rooted in classical sources. While this state of affairs is a product of the very preliminary nature of our research, it is also reflects a complex history of multiple receptions across a range of communities. From the perspective of most contemporary Śrīvidyā practitioners, the Ṣaḍanvayaśāmbhava is simply a specialized mode of esoteric practice, much of it associated with the ritual veneration of the Gurupāduka mantras, reserved for elite initiates. In a similar manner, for Kaulas following either in the tradition of the Kulārṇavatantra or working within the Nepalese Āmnāya system, under the guise of the Ūrdhvāmnāya, late stage initiations reveal the presence of the hidden face of the god Śambhu. Often identified with the non-dual teachings of the upaniṣads, Śambhu presides over the totality of the Śākta systems. Within the vernacular traditions of Telugu, Kannada, and Marathi speaking wandering yogīs and householder practitioners, the tradition of Śambhu or Śāmbhavī vidyā is perceived not as a supplementary mode of tantric ritual, but rather, as a yogic transmission comprising a range of meditative practices, often associated with the use of an internal or external consort. Finally, when it has been noticed at all, western scholars have equated the Śāmbhava with the Ṣaḍanvayaśāmbhava, presenting the practice as a lesser know South-Indian tradition. Such scholarship asserts that the Śāmbhavāmnāya is simply a specialized expression of the Paścimāmnāya. In it, the goddess Kubjikā has been decentered in favor of her male consort Naveśvara or Navātman Bhairava. Over time, it is assumed, this minor tradition was mostly absorbed into Śrividyā.
